cards.title: Ruby2ßhell: Pre-authentication RCE on stock Rails

depth.text: someone found a **string bug** that can let attackers run code on some web apps **without logging in**

cards.title: Distributed, high-performance blob storage on SQLite

depth.text: someone built a **distributed blob store** for **heavy reads and writes** on commodity hardware

Blobasaur is an **open source Rust server** that stores JSON blobs in SQLite, splits them across **shards and nodes**, and speaks the Redis protocol. Its three-node production cluster keeps p99 latency around **2 ms** on every node, though live slot rebalancing and automatic failover aren't implemented yet.

cards.camps: Two camps: the authors say sharding and batching make SQLite work for this workload; critics say SQLite is still a bottleneck and isn't made for it.

comments.text: I spent years trying to squeeze this use case out of sqlite. All roads lead to tears, it is not made for this use case. I wrote https://github.com/anacrolix/possum for this exact use case. It has a few rough edges but it absolutely hauls ass for caching on disk. Incidentally it uses sqlite for transaction/TTL metadata which is more suited to sqlite but it's still the bottleneck. sqlite…

> What we learned along the way… Deleting rows doesn’t shrink SQLite files This is true of every RDBMS I am aware of. It would be horribly inefficient to constantly run page merges in order to be able to free some of them. Whenever I read things on posts that are a. discussed in documentation b. should be apparent from first principles, I immediately lose faith in the product.
I find that partitioning by key range tends to be more flexible and malleable to rebalancing (merge, splits, etc). Doing things like CRC16(key) % 16384 tends to bite eventually.

Earlier in the blog post, Sarat writes about how many databases can't store multi-megabyte blobs. That makes sense to me but later on, he writes > While raw files start to beat SQLite above ~100 KiB, we compress blobs before writing them. And thankfully, 99% of our compressed values sit well below 100 KiB. My question is, were the other databases not tried with compression on the application side?

OpenStack Swift uses SQLite for storing metadata. Each account has one SQLite db. Each container also initially had one SQLite db but in 2018 they added support for sharding so if a container has more than 1 million objects, the container is split into multiple SQLite databases. The performance is not ideal. Ceph scales much better.

cards.title: Software companies are trying to kill home computing?

depth.text: people are arguing whether software companies are pushing home computing toward **renting everything** instead of **owning it**

One commenter says **storage subscriptions** and **high prices** could squeeze enthusiast home computing. Others expect hardware demand to cycle back, while another says **open-source projects** and enthusiasts can keep computing accessible.
